cases.title: newcase
cases.raw_text:
On 12 March 2025 at approximately 8:15 PM, a car driven by Rajesh Kumar struck a pedestrian, Arjun Sharma, at an intersection in Bangalore.

The pedestrian suffered a fractured leg.

Witnesses stated that Rajesh was driving above the speed limit.

Rajesh claims that the traffic signal was malfunctioning and the pedestrian suddenly crossed the road.

CCTV footage shows the vehicle attempting emergency braking moments before impact.

cases.title: newcase2
cases.raw_text:
Two brothers, Ramesh and Suresh, claim ownership of a piece of agricultural land inherited from their father.

Ramesh produced a registered will naming him as the sole beneficiary.

Suresh argues that the will was created under undue influence and presents witnesses claiming the father intended to divide the property equally.

Land records show both brothers have used the property for several years.

cases.title: newcase3
cases.raw_text:
On 5 April 2025, a robbery occurred at a convenience store in Bangalore at approximately 9:30 PM.

The store owner reported that a masked individual entered the store, threatened him, and stole cash worth ₹50,000.

A witness later identified Vikram Sharma as the suspect because he resembled the robber and was seen in the area earlier that evening.

However, CCTV footage from a nearby restaurant shows Vikram dining with friends at the exact time the robbery occurred.

Three independent witnesses, including the restaurant manager, confirmed Vikram's presence at the restaurant.

Mobile phone location records also place Vikram approximately 4 kilometers away from the crime scene during the incident.

No fingerprints, DNA evidence, stolen cash, or other physical evidence were found linking Vikram to the robbery.

The prosecution argues that the eyewitness identification is sufficient to establish guilt.

The defense argues that the CCTV footage, witness testimony, and location records conclusively establish an alibi.

Rohit is accused of assaulting Amit at 9:00 PM.

cases.title: Case 1: Theft Case
cases.raw_text:
Facts
A mobile phone worth ₹80,000 was reported stolen from a college library.
CCTV footage shows Rahul entering the library at 2:10 PM.
The owner left the phone on the table at 2:05 PM.
Rahul was seen leaving the library at 2:15 PM.
The stolen phone was recovered from Rahul's hostel room the next day.
Rahul claims his friend gave him the phone.
Evidence
CCTV footage.
Recovery of phone from accused.
Purchase invoice proving ownership.
Contradiction
Statement A (Rahul): "I have never seen this phone before."
Statement B (Recovery Report): "The phone was found inside Rahul's room."

No evidence places him at the robbery scene.

cases.title: Case 1: Deliberate Shooting After an Argument
cases.raw_text: On the evening of 12 March 2026, Rahul Sharma and Mohan Verma were involved in a heated argument outside a restaurant in Bangalore regarding a financial dispute. Several witnesses reported that Rahul appeared extremely angry and threatened Mohan before leaving the scene. Approximately thirty minutes later, Rahul returned carrying a licensed pistol. CCTV footage from nearby shops captured Rahul approaching Mohan and firing two shots at close range. Mohan collapsed immediately and later died in the hospital. The police recovered the weapon from Rahul's residence, and forensic examination confirmed that the bullets extracted from Mohan's body were fired from the same pistol. During interrogation, Rahul claimed that the weapon discharged accidentally while he was attempting to scare Mohan. However, forensic experts determined that the trigger had been intentionally pulled. Witness testimonies, CCTV footage, ballistic reports, and the prior threat collectively indicate a deliberate act. Therefore, the accused is expected to be found guilty of murder.

cases.title: Case 2: Claim of Self-Defense
cases.raw_text: Late at night, Vikram was returning home when he was confronted by an unknown individual carrying a knife. According to multiple eyewitnesses, the attacker demanded Vikram's wallet and mobile phone. When Vikram refused, the attacker attempted to stab him. In the struggle that followed, Vikram managed to seize a metal rod lying nearby and struck the attacker several times. The attacker suffered severe injuries and later died in the hospital. CCTV footage from a nearby ATM confirms that the deceased initiated the attack and that Vikram attempted to retreat before defending himself. Medical reports show defensive wounds on Vikram's arms consistent with his account. No evidence suggests that Vikram used excessive force beyond what was necessary to protect himself. Based on the available evidence, the act appears to fall within the legal right of private defense

cases.title: Case 4: Builder Fails to Deliver Apartment
cases.raw_text: In 2022, Priya purchased an apartment in a residential project being developed by XYZ Builders. The builder promised possession of the apartment by December 2024, and Priya paid nearly 95% of the agreed amount through documented bank transfers. Despite repeated assurances, construction remained incomplete even by mid-2026. Inspection reports revealed that less than 70% of the project had been completed. Email communications show that the builder continuously postponed delivery dates without providing valid reasons. The builder also continued advertising the same project to new buyers while existing customers remained without possession. Payment receipts, contractual agreements, project registration documents, and progress reports demonstrate a clear failure to fulfill contractual obligations. Therefore, the builder is expected to be held liable for delay and compensation under applicable real estate regulations.

cases.title: Case 5: Dowry Harassment Leading to Suicide
cases.raw_text: Anita married Rakesh in 2023. Within a few months of the marriage, Anita informed her parents that her husband and in-laws were demanding an additional ₹10 lakh and a car as dowry. Over the next year, she repeatedly sent messages describing physical and emotional abuse related to these demands. Her parents also stated that they had transferred money to Rakesh on several occasions in an attempt to resolve the issue. In March 2026, Anita was found dead in her residence after allegedly taking her own life. Investigators recovered WhatsApp chats, voice recordings, and bank transaction records supporting her allegations. Neighbors testified that they frequently heard arguments concerning money and dowry demands. The collected evidence indicates a sustained pattern of harassment directly linked to unlawful dowry demands.

cases.title: State vs Rahul Sharma
cases.raw_text:
On 15 March 2026 at approximately 8:15 PM, a laptop worth ₹85,000 was reported stolen from a software company office in Bengaluru.

A security guard claimed he saw a person resembling Rahul Sharma leaving the building shortly before the theft was discovered.

The prosecution accused Rahul Sharma of committing the theft.

DEFENSE EVIDENCE:

Flight records show Rahul boarded Flight AI-284 from Bengaluru to Delhi at 5:20 PM on the same day.
Airport CCTV footage confirms Rahul entered the departure terminal at 4:10 PM.
Hotel records show Rahul checked into Hotel Grand Delhi at 7:05 PM.
Three independent witnesses confirm Rahul attended a technology conference in Delhi at 8:00 PM.
Mobile tower location records place Rahul in Delhi between 7:00 PM and 11:00 PM.
No fingerprints belonging to Rahul were found at the crime scene.
No stolen property was recovered from Rahul.
No confession was made by Rahul.

In the context of this backend test, if any irregularities or illegal activities were suspected or discovered during the test, the procedure for reporting and investigating such incidents would follow the guidelines set forth in BNSS Section 193.

**Argument:**
The prosecution argues that the evidence presented, including the details of the backend test and its successful outcome, is relevant and admissible. This is based on BSA Section 4, which stipulates that evidence is relevant when facts are connected with the facts in issue under the Act. Furthermore, the procedural aspects of BNSS Section 193, while not directly applicable to the evidence at hand, underscore the legal framework within which such tests and their outcomes are to be considered and acted upon.

**Conclusion:**
In conclusion, the prosecution has built a case that demonstrates the relevance and admissibility of the evidence collected during the backend test. The success of the test, the use of the 'NIM key', and the operation on port 8001 are all pertinent facts that can be connected to the legal framework provided by BSA Section 4 and the procedural guidelines of BNSS Section 193.
